title: Poynting Vector and Electromagnetic Energy Flow
short_intro: The Poynting vector represents the directional energy flux density of an electromagnetic field, quantifying the rate of energy transfer per unit area. It is defined as the cross product of the electric field vector and the magnetic field vector divided by the permeability of free space.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of Poynting vector, its SI units, dimensional formula, and direction of energy propagation in plane electromagnetic waves.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Derivation from Poynting's Theorem, time-averaged Poynting vector for harmonic electromagnetic waves, radiation pressure, and momentum transfer.

prerequisites: Maxwell's equations in differential and integral forms
Vector calculus identities and cross product properties
Energy density in electric and magnetic fields

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Physical Meaning
bullets: The Poynting vector (S) measures the power per unit area transported by electromagnetic fields.

Its direction at any point gives the direction of energy propagation, which is always perpendicular to both the electric field (E) and magnetic field (B) vectors in the sense of a right-handed screw (E x B).
It accounts for the flow of electromagnetic energy into or out of a given volume.

concept_notes.heading: Poynting's Theorem and Energy Conservation
bullets: Poynting's theorem represents the law of conservation of energy for a system of electromagnetic fields and charges.
The rate of work done by the fields on charges plus the time rate of change of electromagnetic energy density equals the negative divergence of the Poynting vector.
Mathematically expressed as the continuity equation for electromagnetic energy: del dot S + dU/dt = -J dot E.

concept_notes.heading: Time-Averaged Poynting Vector
bullets: For sinusoidal electromagnetic waves, the instantaneous Poynting vector oscillates at twice the frequency of the wave.
The observable quantity in most optical and microwave experiments is the time-averaged magnitude, known as the intensity of the wave.
Expressed as S<sub>avg</sub> = (1/2) c epsilon<sub>0</sub> E<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> or in terms of rms values as E<sub>rms</sub> B<sub>rms</sub> / mu<sub>0</sub>.

concept_notes.heading: Radiation Pressure
bullets: Electromagnetic waves carry linear momentum in addition to energy, related to the Poynting vector by p = S / c<sup>2</sup> per unit volume.
When an electromagnetic wave is completely absorbed by a surface, the radiation pressure is given by P = S<sub>avg</sub> / c.
For total reflection at normal incidence, the radiation pressure is doubled: P = 2S<sub>avg</sub> / c.

derivations.title: Derivation of Poynting's Theorem from Maxwell's Equations
derivations.conditions: Free space or linear isotropic medium without magnetic or dielectric hysteresis
steps: Start with Maxwell's curl equations: curl E = -dB/dt and curl H = J + dD/dt.
Take the dot product of H with curl E and E with curl H, then subtract the two equations: H dot (curl E) - E dot (curl H) = -H dot (dB/dt) - E dot J - E dot (dD/dt).
Use the vector identity div (E x H) = H dot (curl E) - E dot (curl H).
Substitute constitutive relations B = mu H and D = epsilon E, yielding div (E x H) = -E dot J - d/dt [ (1/2)epsilon E<sup>2</sup> + (1/2)mu H<sup>2</sup> ].
derivations.result: div S + dU/dt = -J dot E, where S = E x H and U = (1/2)(epsilon E<sup>2</sup> + mu H<sup>2</sup>).

derivations.title: Time-Averaged Poynting Vector for Harmonic Plane Waves
derivations.conditions: Monochromatic plane electromagnetic wave propagating in vacuum
steps: Express electric and magnetic fields as real parts of complex harmonic waves: E = E<sub>0</sub> cos(kz - omega t) i and B = B<sub>0</sub> cos(kz - omega t) j.
Write the instantaneous Poynting vector S = (1/mu<sub>0</sub>) (E x B) = (E<sub>0</sub> B<sub>0</sub> / mu<sub>0</sub>) cos<sup>2</sup>(kz - omega t) k.
Take the time average over a full cycle: <cos<sup>2</sup>(kz - omega t)> = 1/2.
Substitute B<sub>0</sub> = E<sub>0</sub> / c and c = 1 / sqrt(mu<sub>0</sub> epsilon<sub>0</sub>).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Sinusoidal Variation of E, B, and Instantaneous S
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot showing E and B waves in phase along z-axis, and a strictly positive double-frequency curve representing the instantaneous Poynting vector magnitude S versus z or t.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that energy flows continuously in one direction even though the individual field vectors oscillate and reverse sign.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Multiple choice questions testing the frequency of energy oscillation relative to field frequency (2ω).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Nichols Radiometer Experiment Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A suspended torsion mirror setup where a light beam is directed onto a reflecting or absorbing vane inside an evacuated bulb.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Directly measures radiation pressure exerted by light, verifying the momentum flux predicted by the Poynting vector formulation.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual and numerical questions on radiation force and pressure calculations.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Energy Flow in a Current-Carrying Resistor (Poynting's Conundrum)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A cylindrical resistor with radial electric field lines pointing inward/outward and azimuthal magnetic field lines looping around it, resulting in Poynting vectors entering the resistor surface radially.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that electrical energy does not flow primarily through the wire material as kinetic energy of electrons, but enters laterally from the surrounding fields as Poynting flux to dissipate as Joule heat.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Advanced PGT conceptual questions on the microscopic path of energy delivery in DC circuits.

solved_numericals.question: The peak value of the electric field in a plane electromagnetic wave is 300 V/m. Calculate the maximum value of the Poynting vector.
solution_steps: Identify given values: E_0 = 300 V/m, c = 3 x 10^8 m/s, epsilon_0 = 8.85 x 10^-12 C^2/N m^2.
Recall relation for maximum Poynting vector magnitude: S_max = (1/2) c epsilon_0 E_0^2.

solved_numericals.question: A laser beam has a power of 15 mW and a beam radius of 1.0 mm. Assuming the intensity is uniformly distributed across the beam cross-section, find the peak electric field of the electromagnetic wave.
solution_steps: Calculate the area of the beam cross-section: A = pi r^2 = 3.1416 * (1.0 x 10^-3)^2 = 3.1416 x 10^-6 m^2.
Calculate the average intensity (S_avg): S_avg = Power / Area = (15 x 10^-3) / (3.1416 x 10^-6) = 4.775 x 10^3 W/m^2.
Relate intensity to peak electric field: S_avg = (1/2) c epsilon_0 E_0^2.
Rearrange for E_0: E_0 = sqrt( 2 * S_avg / (c * epsilon_0 ) ).

solved_numericals.question: A parallel beam of monochromatic light of intensity 500 W/m^2 falls on a perfectly absorbing surface of area 2.0 m^2 at normal incidence for 10 minutes. Calculate the total momentum delivered to the surface.
solution_steps: Calculate total energy delivered to the surface: U = S_avg * A * t = 500 * 2.0 * (10 * 60) = 600,000 J.
Relate momentum (p) to energy (U) for complete absorption: p = U / c.
Substitute values: p = 600,000 / (3 x 10^8) = 2.0 x 10^-3 kg m/s.

assumptions_and_limitations: The macroscopic definition assumes continuous media where local field averages hold true.
Constitutive relations D = epsilon E and B = mu H are assumed linear and isotropic unless tensor forms are specified.
In dispersive media, the simple algebraic expression for the energy density and Poynting vector requires modification to account for frequency-dependent permittivity.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The Poynting vector gives the direction of motion of individual electric charges in an electromagnetic wave.
common_misconceptions.correct: The Poynting vector gives the direction of flow of electromagnetic energy, not the trajectories of charged particles.
common_misconceptions.why: Energy flux describes field transport through space, whereas particle motion depends on the Lorentz force acting on specific charges.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Energy in a current-carrying wire flows entirely inside the copper wire as kinetic energy of conduction electrons.
common_misconceptions.correct: A major portion of electromagnetic energy flows through the space surrounding the wire via the Poynting vector and enters the wire laterally.
common_misconceptions.why: Poynting's theorem reveals that the electric field along the wire and the azimuthal magnetic field outside produce an inward-directed Poynting vector.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The instantaneous Poynting vector is always constant in time for a continuous wave.
common_misconceptions.correct: The instantaneous Poynting vector oscillates between zero and a maximum value at twice the frequency of the wave.
common_misconceptions.why: Because it depends on the product of field oscillations, cos^2(wt), it pulses at double frequency, though detectors measure the time average.

quick_revision: Poynting vector S = (1/mu_0)(E x B) measures directional electromagnetic energy flux in W/m^2.
Time-averaged intensity for harmonic waves is S_avg = (1/2) c epsilon_0 E_0^2.
Radiation pressure for complete absorption is P = S_avg / c, and for total reflection it is 2S_avg / c.
